title: The Test Pyramid: Unit, Integration and End-to-End
oneLiner: What each level of test proves, what it costs, and why most of a healthy suite is small fast tests.
keyTakeaway: Unit tests check one piece of logic in isolation and run in milliseconds. Integration tests check that your code works with real collaborators such as a database or the HTTP pipeline. End-to-end tests drive the whole system the way a user does. Moving up the pyramid buys confidence that the parts fit together, and costs speed, reliability and how precisely a failure points at the bug. So write many unit tests, fewer integration tests and a handful of end-to-end tests for the journeys that must never break.
explanation:
A unit test exercises a small piece of behaviour, usually a method or a class, with nothing slow or shared involved: no database, network, file system or clock. It runs in milliseconds, gives the same result every time, and when it fails the name tells you exactly what broke. An integration test checks that your code works with something real it depends on: the SQL your repository generates against a real database (often in a container), or an ASP.NET Core endpoint through the real routing, model binding and middleware using WebApplicationFactory. An end-to-end (E2E) test runs the deployed system from the outside, for example a Playwright script that signs in, adds to a basket and checks out in a real browser.

Mike Cohn's test pyramid says to have many tests at the bottom and few at the top. Higher tests catch the bugs that live between components (a misconfigured connection string, a JSON field renamed on one side), but they're slower, need more setup, fail for reasons unrelated to your change (timeouts, test data, a flaky browser), and a red E2E test can mean almost anything. The inverted shape, mostly manual and E2E tests with few unit tests, is called the ice-cream cone, and it produces a slow, flaky build that people learn to rerun rather than read. Some teams prefer Kent C. Dodds' testing trophy, which puts the most weight on integration tests; the shared point is to put each check at the lowest level that can catch the bug.

Every test, at any level, has the same three parts, called arrange, act, assert (AAA). Arrange builds the inputs and the object under test. Act performs the single behaviour being tested. Assert checks the outcome. Keeping one act per test means a failure points at one behaviour, and naming tests after the behaviour, such as Withdraw_MoreThanBalance_Throws, makes the test list read like a specification.

In C#, xUnit is the most common framework in new .NET projects (NUnit and MSTest are the others). A [Fact] is a test with no parameters; a [Theory] runs once per [InlineData] row. xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test, so the constructor is per-test setup and Dispose is teardown, and tests can't leak state through fields. Shared expensive setup, such as one database container for a whole class, goes in a fixture via IClassFixture<T>. Run everything with dotnet test.

Interview answer to "how would you test this?": unit tests for the logic and edge cases, an integration test for each boundary (database, external API, message queue) and one or two end-to-end tests for the critical path, then say why each level belongs where it is.
